newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat warns of chaos if U.S. takes peace timeout.
newsitem.headline: Arafat warns of chaos if U.S. takes peace timeout.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in an interview published on Wednesday the Middle East was headed for "the abyss" if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies were not blocked.
He warned that if Washington chose to stand back for a time from the process it has sponsored since peace talks began in 1991, the region could be "dragged into chaos".
Arafat vowed to impose the death penalty on people who sold land to Israelis, a move that has raised Washington's ire.

"Netanyahu is destroying the peace process between Israel and the Arabs and the entire region is facing severe events. Netanyahu is systematically violating the accords and he will bear responsibility for what happens. He is scorning the entire world," Arafat was quoted by Yedioth Ahronoth daily as saying.
"Everything is collapsing in front of our eyes. There is no power that will stop the prime minister of Israel, and we are continuing to march toward the abyss," Arafat said.
Arafat criticised U.S. vetoes of U.N. resolutions against Israel's building a new 6,500-home Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in 1967 and later annexed.
But he said he believed U.S. policy on settlements was closer to the Palestinian view than to that of Netanyahu.
"The Americans can activate their influence and pressure and then we'll see everything clearly, that their opinion is not comfortable with Netanyahu.
"They also could stop their involvement in the conflict for a time, and then the danger would exist that we'll be dragged into chaos," Arafat said.

Arafat sent President Bill Clinton a letter on Friday saying U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross's latest mission failed and asked Clinton to intervene personally. Washington said now was not the time for dramatic intervention.
Peacemaking halted when the settlement construction began on March 18. On March 21, a Palestinian militant opposed to peace killed himself and three Israelis in a Tel Aviv cafe bombing.

Palestinians demand an end to settlement building before resuming peace talks. Netanyahu, who refuses to halt the construction, demands the PLO do more to curb militants. Arafat says he is already fighting "terror".
Asked if negotiations could resume if work stopped on the new settlement, Arafat said: "That would be a positive signal that would contribute to renewal of the (peace) process".
Arafat said he stood behind a recent Palestinian Authority decision to enforce an old Jordanian law in the West Bank imposing the death penalty for land sales to Jews.
"We are talking about isolated traitors," Arafat said. "And we will impose against them what is on the law books. That is our right and our obligation to protect our land."
Israel has linked the ban on land sales to Israelis with the killings of two Palestinian land dealers found dead in the West Bank. The Authority has denied any involvement in the killings.
The Palestinians see Jewish settlement building as pre-empting "final status" peace talks which have yet to resume since Netanyahu took power in June 1996.
